meta.title: Agents. Set Up and Lead — course 3 · AIVIS.ONE
meta.desc: A free AIVIS.ONE course: how to lead a project with three levels of agents, give tasks, accept results and move the work to a new chat without losing anything.
s01.t03: In this course you will learn to
s01.t04: build a project on three levels in your own folder
s01.t05: give a worker a task from a template and accept the result by report and check
s01.t06: move the work to a new chat without losing anything
s02.t02: Big work is a project: it needs a folder, not one long chat
s02.t04: “Let us discuss everything about the book exchange here”
s02.t05: The longer it runs, the more junk piles up: rejected versions, edits, side topics. The model (the program that writes the chat's answers) gets confused and forgets.
s02.t08: one chat will not finish it
s02.t10: the result is not one document
s02.t16: in a day or a week
s02.t17: One task lives in a chat. A project lives in a folder: chats come and go.
s03.t01: AI as a member of staff
s03.t02: An agent does exactly what you asked, and no more
s03.t03: A vague task misses the goal. An agent (a chat you gave a role and a task that carries out the steps itself) will not do what you did not name.
s03.t04: No control, no result. An agent remembers only what is in front of it (its context) and the files.
s03.t05: No feedback, no improvement. Once finished, the agent forgets you.
s03.t06: A rough first version is raw material: criticising it is easier than writing from scratch. The goal, the numbers and what becomes a task are yours to decide.
s04.t07: The whole: the goal everything else serves
s04.t10: An intermediate result that is checked before moving on
s04.t11: announcement, schedule and rules are ready
s04.t15: One chat, one task: materials go in, a known result comes out. Two tasks in one chat get mixed up.
s05.t02: Three levels of agents, and you above them
s05.t04: Agents, top to bottom, each a separate chat with its own role
s05.t05: The navigator leads, holds one plan, asks you where a choice has to be made (a fork in the road), and never edits the work itself
s05.t06: The orchestrator plans and is the only one who changes files
s05.t07: Workers do one task each and end
s05.t12: In our example you are the owner, the navigator leads the preparation, the orchestrator prepares the files, a worker checks the dates. Whoever produces does not judge.
s06.t02: The navigator leads: one plan and questions at forks
s06.t03: One plan: a single place that says what comes next. There is no second list.
s06.t04: A task needs your yes: before it, a proposal; after it, an obligation.
s06.t05: A question to you has four parts: the question; the context; three options with a plus and a minus; its own argued answer.
s06.t06: Accepts after a check, and hands big work to the orchestrator instead of editing it itself.
s06.t07: While a question to you is open, the work that depends on it does not start: work done before the answer gets redone.
s07.t02: The orchestrator changes files, a worker does one task
s07.t07: Gives the orchestrator an assignment (the overall job), accepts the result
s07.t10: Plans the assignment, writes each worker a brief (a written instruction), calls them and checks their reports
s07.t11: the only one who changes them
s07.t13: One task from a written brief, then ends
s07.t15: A worker does not plan, widen the task or decide for you: at a fork it returns the question.
s08.t02: A stage: start, work, result, check
s08.t03: Start: what must happen for the stage to start. Example: you approved the date and place.
s08.t04: Work: several work chats, one task in each.
s08.t05: Result: the files left in the folder: announcement, schedule, rules.
s08.t06: Check: a concrete criterion, not “seems fine”: three files in place, dates checked, no contradictions.
s08.t07: Only tasks that change different files run side by side. Two tasks on one file overwrite each other.
s09.t02: The project folder is the memory, a chat is a consumable
s09.t03: Everything important leaves the chat for the folder. What was not taken out is lost to the project.
s09.t04: A result is something you can open: a file, a table or a written decision. No such result, the task is not closed.
s09.t05: The pointer file at the top level of the folder: stages and their status, key files, open questions. A new chat gets up to speed from it.
s09.t06: A month on, you open the book exchange folder and from the pointer file understand in a minute where you stopped.
s10.t02: The folder template and the roles card
s10.t03: Practice: set up the book exchange project folder in one hour
s10.t04: The folder template: the pointer file “Start here”, the files “Plan”, “Decisions”, “Questions” and the folders “Work”, “Reports”, “Summaries”.
s10.t05: The roles card: owner, navigator, orchestrator, worker on one sheet: what each does and what each never does.
s11.t02: An agent's rules must arrive by themselves, not by request
s11.t05: The agent may skip it, you may forget. Not read, and the work carries on as if nothing happened.
s11.t08: an assistant on your computer reads the rules file by itself as soon as you point it at the project folder; a plain chat does not do this, so paste the file as your first message (see slide 12)
s11.t10: rules only, no history and no stories
s11.t14: ask first thing which rules the chat has loaded
s11.t15: If the rules did not arrive, the agent works with no plan. So the first question to a new chat: “Which rules have you loaded?” Assistants on your computer do this (slide 12); in a plain chat, paste the rules file as your first message.
s12.t02: Three places to work, from simple to strong
s12.t07: One task; nothing is kept between conversations
s12.t08: you need a one-off text or answer
s12.t09: A chat with files and projects
s12.t10: Keeps the materials and instructions of a project
s12.t11: you lead a project of several documents yourself
s12.t13: Reads and changes files in the folder you choose, runs several workers
s12.t14: you need the three levels of this course
s12.t15: Do not climb higher than the task needs.
s12.t16: If you do not have an assistant on your computer, do the practice in three plain chats: copy the files between them by hand, and the orchestrator sends you the finished text of each file. Product features change: check the product's own description.
s13.t03: A worker knows only what you wrote in the brief: what is not there does not exist for it
s13.t04: 1. Goal and how to tell it is done: one sentence on what must exist, and a clear way to check it is done.
s13.t05: 2. Context and inputs: 3 to 5 facts this task needs, and the files to read first.
s13.t06: 3. What you may change, and what you must not: the exact list; working notes in one place, deleted before the end; if a decision is needed, stop and return it.
s13.t07: 4. Steps or constraints: numbered steps, or limits: length, tone, allowed sources.
s13.t08: 5. What to hand back: the files and a report in the seven-field shape.
s14.t03: Take the assignment from the navigator and write down what the output must be.
s14.t04: Cut it into tasks and write a brief for each from the template.
s14.t05: Start the workers: together if they touch no common file, otherwise one after another.
s14.t06: Wait for all of them and check their reports itself, not take them on trust.
s14.t07: Make the changes to the files and hand the result to the navigator as a report.
s14.t08: One cycle, one assignment. A decision that is not its own, the orchestrator returns to the navigator.
s15.t02: Handing work back: a report of seven fields
s15.t03: The report reads in seconds, and a gap in it shows at once
s15.t04: The same seven fields every time: 1. what was done; 2. files changed; 3. how it was checked; 4. what was not done; 5. open questions; 6. risks; 7. status. Write “none” only after you looked.
s15.t05: Five honest statuses: DONE, FAILED, CANNOT VERIFY, PARTIAL, BLOCKED (cannot go on without your decision or someone else's file). FAILED, CANNOT VERIFY and BLOCKED are honest answers; never upgraded to DONE because the claim sounds plausible.
s16.t02: Whoever produces does not judge; a check can be repeated
s16.t03: Another party judges: a fresh chat or you. A chat does not catch its own blind spots.
s16.t04: A check can be repeated: claim, how it was checked, result, status side by side. “Looks fine” is not a check.
s16.t05: “No errors” counts only if the check can find them: plant a known error and make sure it is found.
s16.t06: The worker writes: “all dates match”. The orchestrator runs the check itself and plants a date that is known to be wrong. If it is not found, “no errors” means nothing.
s17.t03: All eight, every time: one fails and the work goes back with the check number and the reason
s17.t04: 1. the result matches the brief's criterion for done; 2. it was checked by someone who did not make it.
s17.t05: 3. the check can be repeated; 4. it is clear how much was checked and how we made sure the check works.
s17.t06: 5. nothing changed outside the allowed scope; 6. every figure says where it came from and when it was taken.
s17.t07: 7. open questions and returned decisions went to the owner; 8. the plan and the pointer file are updated.
s18.t02: A tired chat: move it, do not repair it
s18.t03: Every agent's memory is finite. A chat that drifted is not repaired: it is replaced by a new one.
s18.t04: A hand-over summary (snapshot) of seven parts: goal; decisions taken; where things stand now; next step; open questions; files to read first; what went wrong. Take figures and file names from the folder, not from the chat's memory.
s18.t05: Only the next chat can test the hand-over summary, not its writer: have the new chat say where the project stands. Keep the old one open to answer questions, but give it no work.
s19.t02: Prepare the book exchange on three levels
s19.t03: Folder: create it from the template and fill in the pointer file.
s19.t04: Navigator (first chat): state the goal, let it draw a plan of three stages and ask you about date and place. Answer before work starts.
s19.t05: Orchestrator (second chat; best in an assistant on your computer, see slide 12): assign the announcement, the schedule and a list of rules; let it change the files.
s19.t06: Worker (third chat): from a five-block brief, check the dates and find contradictions; a report in seven fields.
s19.t07: Acceptance: the navigator accepts after a check. Whatever is yours, you decide.
s19.t08: How it went. The course author answered and checked in the owner's place. The navigator held the task until three questions were answered. The orchestrator added “tea” on its own. The worker only read the dates (14 of 14), without a rule-based check. A new navigator returned the work: a return is a normal outcome.
s20.t08: move to a new chat from the hand-over summary and the pointer file
s20.t11: close the chat that mixed levels; briefs from the template
s20.t14: stop, tidy up, rewrite the pointer file from what is there
s20.t15: You do not remember where you stopped
s20.t17: a strong signal: check the folder against the pointer file
s20.t18: One sign is normal; two or three together mean act. The owner's good habits: do not treasure chats, do not mix levels or tasks, do not carry unfinished things forward, keep the pointer file.
s21.t09: Leads you from a task to a finished skill (course 2).
s21.t12: Two files and a note on how to run them.
s21.t15: Six files: roles, folder, brief, hand-back, checklist, hand-over summary.
s21.t17: Next, course 4: we launch a small project by a strict order of work (a protocol).
s22.t01: Nothing irreversible happens without your yes: no payment, signature, deletion or publication
s22.t02: A public test version of SANKORD comes out in November 2026. It is a test: the system may update often and break. The working version of SANKORD comes out in January 2027.
s22.t03: Pre-order is open: pre-order holders get an early version in December 2026 and the working version from January 2027.
